analysis.one_liner: Creates a Medicare-based public health insurance option and lets Medicare negotiate drug prices.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its first committee referral; it received one subcommittee hearing and died in the 116th Congress without any committee or floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The Choose Medicare Act would have created "Medicare Part E" — a government-run public health insurance plan that anyone could buy on the insurance exchanges, that employers could offer their workers, and that workers could keep even if they lost their jobs. It also would have required Medicare to negotiate prescription drug prices for the first time, capped seniors' out-of-pocket Medicare costs at $6,700 a year, and made insurance subsidies much more generous — extending them to families earning up to six times the poverty level and reducing what low- and middle-income families pay out of pocket. The bill was referred to three House committees, got a single subcommittee hearing, and never received a vote of any kind.
analysis.who_benefits: People buying insurance on the exchanges would gain a public plan option with gold-level coverage, and families earning up to 600% of the poverty level would become eligible for premium tax credits benchmarked to more generous gold plans [S2][S3]. Low- and middle-income exchange enrollees would get sharply reduced deductibles and copays [S3]. Medicare beneficiaries would gain an annual out-of-pocket cap ($6,700 starting in 2021) that traditional Medicare lacks, and lower drug prices from required HHS negotiation [S3]. Workers who lose a job could keep their Part E coverage, and employers would get a voluntary public plan to offer workers plus navigator referrals for employees whose coverage is unaffordable [S3][S2]. States would get $30 billion for reinsurance and help with enrollees' out-of-pocket costs [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Exchange enrollees, Medicare beneficiaries, and uninsured Americans

how_it_helps.text: Creates Medicare Part E public health plans available in the individual, small-group, and large-group markets, sold on the exchanges with gold-level coverage, so people who find private plans unaffordable or inadequate have a government-run alternative
Lets workers keep their public plan after being laid off or changing jobs, an unusual portability feature no current employer coverage provides

Caps annual out-of-pocket costs for traditional Medicare at $6,700 starting in 2021, closing a gap that leaves the roughly two-thirds of seniors in traditional Medicare with unlimited cost-sharing today
Repeals the law barring Medicare from negotiating drug prices and requires HHS to negotiate; if talks fail after a year, the price falls to the lower of what the VA pays for the drug
Expands premium tax credits by raising the eligibility ceiling from 400% to 600% of the poverty level and benchmarking the credit to the second-lowest-cost gold plan instead of silver
Cuts deductibles and copays for exchange enrollees earning up to 400% of poverty, with plans covering up to 94% of costs for the lowest-income households
Provides $30 billion to states over 2020–2022 for reinsurance or direct help with premiums, copays, and deductibles

Requires HHS or state regulators to take corrective action — denying, modifying, or ordering rebates for — excessive or unjustified insurance rates, and extends the ACA's community-rating rules to large employer plans
Requires employers to refer workers whose coverage is unaffordable or thin to enrollment navigators, and funds more navigators

analysis.who_pays: Private health insurers would face a government-run competitor in every market, tighter rating rules, and rate review with mandatory corrective actions [S2][S3]. Brand-name drug makers would lose pricing power under required Medicare negotiation with a VA-price fallback [S3]. Taxpayers would fund $2 billion in startup costs, initial claim reserves, and the $30 billion reinsurance fund, plus the cost of richer subsidies for more families [S3]. Employers would bear a new duty to refer employees to navigators and see community-rating rules extended to large-group plans [S2][S3]. Hospitals and doctors would be paid no more than average exchange rates and could not balance-bill public plan patients [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Private insurers, drug makers, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The bill appropriates $2 billion in startup funding, open-ended claim reserves, and $30 billion for a reinsurance and affordability fund, and the expanded premium credits — with eligibility stretched to 600% of the poverty level — add substantial ongoing federal cost on top

Part E premiums must fully finance the plan's benefit and administrative costs, so if the public plan attracted a sicker, older pool of enrollees its premiums could climb, and a required rate floor of no less than Medicare payment rates limits how cheaply it could compete

The public plan must cover abortion and all other reproductive services, state bans on such coverage would not apply to it, and the bill explicitly overrides restrictions on using federal funds for reproductive health services — a provision that guaranteed intense opposition and likely narrow any coalition of support

Provider participation is mandatory for existing Medicare providers, and payment rates are capped at average exchange rates with balance billing prohibited, which hospitals and physician groups would argue squeezes their revenue to subsidize the new plan

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer benefits are broad and concrete: a public option in every insurance market, job-loss portability, a real out-of-pocket cap for traditional Medicare, Medicare drug negotiation, and far richer subsidies and cost-sharing help. The costs are real but moderate relative to the coverage provided — roughly $32 billion in explicit appropriations plus ongoing subsidy spending — and the bill's design limits taxpayer exposure by requiring the public plan to self-finance through premiums. Its biggest weakness is political rather than fiscal: the abortion-coverage mandate and federal funding override guaranteed a fight the bill, with only eight sponsors, was never positioned to win.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee — sent to three committees on the day it was introduced, heard once in a subcommittee, and never marked up or voted on before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Cedric Richmond introduced the Choose Medicare Act on May 1, 2019, joined by Rep. Jared Huffman and Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton; seven House Democrats cosponsored it in total

The same day, the House referred it to three committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and Labor — splitting it among committees with jurisdiction over health, taxes, and employer benefits
It was sent to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee on May 2, 2019
The subcommittee held a hearing on December 10, 2019 — the only committee activity the bill ever received
No committee ever marked it up or voted on it, no floor vote ever occurred, and the bill expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers and brand-name drug makers are better off: they keep their markets free of a public competitor and Medicare remains barred from negotiating drug prices. The status quo also spares taxpayers the bill's $32 billion in new appropriations and expanded subsidies.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private health insurers and drug makers

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held on the bill; all of its recorded support was Democratic — one sponsor and seven Democratic cosponsors, with no Republican support.

industries.note: A Medicare Part E public plan would have competed against private insurers in the individual, small-group, and large-group markets with guaranteed provider networks, no balance billing, and HHS as the regulator of rates. Insurers would also face mandatory corrective action on rates they set and an extension of community-rating rules to large-group plans, though a $30 billion state reinsurance fund would have partly offset their risk.

The bill repeals the 'noninterference' provision that bars Medicare from negotiating drug prices and requires HHS to negotiate, with a fallback that sets the price at the lower of what the VA pays. It also applies the negotiated prices to the new public plan's drug coverage.

Every existing Medicare provider would automatically be in-network for the public plan, guaranteeing access to a new pool of patients, but payment rates could not exceed average exchange rates, balance billing would be barred, and rates could not fall below Medicare levels.

Employers would gain a voluntary public plan they could offer workers in the group market, but they would carry a new duty to refer employees to enrollment navigators when their coverage is unaffordable, and community-rating rules would extend to large-group plans.
